problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
Summary**

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
The minimum possible number of rectangular tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}=2\cdot2025-2 .
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Permutation viewpoint.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit
   square, the uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a
   bijection \(\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that
   the unique uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).

2. **Construction attaining \(2n-2\) tiles.**  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) (the uncovered squares lie on
   the main diagonal).  
   *For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) place a **vertical** tile*
   \[
   V_j=\{(r,j):j+1\le r\le n\},
   \]
   i.e. a rectangle of size \((n-j)\times1\) covering the cells strictly
   below the diagonal in column \(j\).  
   *For each row \(i\) with \(1\le i\le n-1\) place a **horizontal** tile*
   \[
   H_i=\{(i,c):i+1\le c\le n\},
   \]
   i.e. a rectangle of size \(1\times (n-i)\) covering the cells strictly
   to the right of the diagonal in row \(i\).  
   The \(n-1\) vertical tiles and the \(n-1\) horizontal tiles are pairwise
   disjoint, avoid all diagonal squares, and together cover every
   non‑diagonal unit square.  Hence the construction uses exactly
   \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) tiles.

3. **Universal lower bound \(2n-2\).**  
   For an arbitrary permutation \(\pi\) define, for each row \(i\),

   \[
   L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j<\pi(i)\},\qquad
   R_i=\{(i,j):\pi(i)<j\le n\},
   \]

   the cells left and right of the uncovered square in that row.
   Any tile that meets a cell of \(L_i\) cannot meet a cell of \(R_i\)
   (otherwise it would also contain the hole \((i,\pi(i))\)).  
   Consequently the set of all tiles splits into a **left family**
   \(\mathcal L\) (tiles contained in \(\bigcup_i L_i\)) and a **right
   family** \(\mathcal R\) (tiles contained in \(\bigcup_i R_i\)).  The two
   families are disjoint, so  

   \[
   |\text{tiles}|=|\mathcal L|+|\mathcal R|.
   \]

   *Left side.*  
   Consider the rows with a non‑empty left block, i.e. those with
   \(\pi(i)>1\).  List them as \(i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k}\) with
   \(\pi(i_1)<\pi(i_2)<\dots <\pi(i_k)\); here \(k=n-1\) because exactly
   one row (the one with \(\pi(i)=1\)) has an empty left block.
   For each \(t\) the cell  

   \[
   c_t=(i_t,\;\pi(i_t)-1)\in L_{i_t}
   \]

   is the rightmost cell of the left block of row \(i_t\).
   Any tile of \(\mathcal L\) that appears **before** row \(i_t\) and also
   meets \(L_{i_t}\) must have its column interval contained in
   \(\{1,\dots ,\pi(i_t)-2\}\); otherwise it would contain the hole
   \((i_t,\pi(i_t))\).  Hence such a tile cannot cover \(c_t\).  Therefore
   a new tile of \(\mathcal L\) is forced for each \(t\), and the tiles
   required for distinct \(t\) are distinct (their column intervals end at
   different values \(\pi(i_t)-1\)).  Thus  

   \[
   |\mathcal L|\ge k=n-1 .
   \]

   *Right side.*  
   The argument is symmetric.  List the rows with a non‑empty right block,
   i.e. those with \(\pi(j)<n\), as \(j_1,j_2,\dots ,j_{\ell}\) with
   \(\pi(j_1)>\pi(j_2)>\dots >\pi(j_{\ell})\); again \(\ell=n-1\).
   For each \(t\) the cell  

   \[
   d_t=(j_t,\;\pi(j_t)+1)\in R_{j_t}
   \]

   is the leftmost cell of the right block of row \(j_t\).
   Any earlier tile of \(\mathcal R\) meeting \(R_{j_t}\) must have its
   column interval contained in \(\{\pi(j_t)+2,\dots ,n\}\), so it cannot
   cover \(d_t\).  Consequently a new tile of \(\mathcal R\) is forced for
   each \(t\), giving  

   \[
   |\mathcal R|\ge \ell=n-1 .
   \]

   Adding the two independent bounds yields  

   \[
   |\text{tiles}|\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
   \]

4. **Conclusion.**  
   The explicit tiling of step 2 uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, and step 3
   proves that no tiling can use fewer.  Hence the minimum possible number
   of tiles is  

   \[
   2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
   \]

---

**Detailed Solution**

Let \(n=2025\).  
Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit
square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists
a bijection \(\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the unique
uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  A tiling with \(2n-2\) tiles

Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\).  
For each column \(j\) with \(1\le j\le n-1\) place the vertical tile  

\[
V_j=\{(r,j):j+1\le r\le n\},
\]

which is a rectangle of size \((n-j)\times1\).  
For each row \(i\) with \(1\le i\le n-1\) place the horizontal tile  

\[
H_i=\{(i,c):i+1\le c\le n\},
\]

which is a rectangle of size \(1\times (n-i)\).

*Disjointness.*  
\(V_j\) occupies column \(j\) and rows \(>j\); \(H_i\) occupies row \(i\)
and columns \(>i\).  A cell could belong to both a vertical and a
horizontal tile only if it satisfied \(r>c\) and \(c>r\) simultaneously,
which is impossible.  Hence the tiles are pairwise disjoint.

*Avoidance of uncovered squares.*  
The uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).  None of the
vertical tiles contains a cell with column equal to its row index, because
\(V_j\) uses rows \(>j\).  None of the horizontal tiles contains a cell
with row equal to its column index, because \(H_i\) uses columns \(>i\).
Thus every diagonal cell remains uncovered.

*Coverage.*  
Every non‑diagonal cell either lies strictly below the diagonal (so it is
in some \(V_j\)) or strictly above the diagonal (so it is in some
\(H_i\)).  Consequently all unit squares except the diagonal are covered.

The number of tiles is  

\[
| \{V_j\}_{j=1}^{n-1}|+| \{H_i\}_{i=1}^{n-1}|=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A universal lower bound

For an arbitrary permutation \(\pi\) define, for each row \(i\),

\[
L_i=\{(i,j):1\le j<\pi(i)\},\qquad
R_i=\{(i,j):\pi(i)<j\le n\}.
\]

A tile that meets a cell of \(L_i\) cannot meet a cell of \(R_i\), because
otherwise it would also contain the hole \((i,\pi(i))\).  Hence the set of
all tiles splits into two disjoint families:

* \(\mathcal L\): tiles contained entirely in \(\bigcup_i L_i\);
* \(\mathcal R\): tiles contained entirely in \(\bigcup_i R_i\).

Thus  

\[
\#\text{tiles}=|\mathcal L|+|\mathcal R|.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.1  At least \(n-1\) left‑side tiles

Rows with a non‑empty left block are precisely those with \(\pi(i)>1\);
there are \(n-1\) of them.  List these rows as  

\[
i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k}\qquad(k=n-1)
\]

so that  

\[
\pi(i_1)<\pi(i_2)<\dots <\pi(i_k).
\]

For each \(t\) consider the cell  

\[
c_t=(i_t,\;\pi(i_t)-1)\in L_{i_t},
\]

the rightmost cell of the left block of row \(i_t\).

Suppose a tile \(U\in\mathcal L\) that appears **before** row \(i_t\)
covers a cell of \(L_{i_t}\).  Because \(U\) is a rectangle, its column
interval is an interval \([a,b]\).  If \(b\ge\pi(i_t)-1\), then column
\(\pi(i_t)\) would also belong to the interval, forcing \(U\) to contain
the hole \((i_t,\pi(i_t))\), which is impossible.  Hence any such tile
must satisfy \(b\le\pi(i_t)-2\) and therefore cannot cover the cell
\(c_t\).  Consequently a new tile of \(\mathcal L\) is required for each
\(t\).  The tiles forced for different values of \(t\) are distinct,
because their rightmost columns \(\pi(i_t)-1\) are distinct.  Hence  

\[
|\mathcal L|\ge k=n-1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.2  At least \(n-1\) right‑side tiles

The symmetric argument deals with rows having a non‑empty right block,
i.e. those with \(\pi(j)<n\); there are again \(n-1\) of them.  List them
as  

\[
j_1,j_2,\dots ,j_{\ell}\qquad(\ell=n-1)
\]

with  

\[
\pi(j_1)>\pi(j_2)>\dots >\pi(j_{\ell}).
\]

For each \(t\) the cell  

\[
d_t=(j_t,\;\pi(j_t)+1)\in R_{j_t}
\]

is the leftmost cell of the right block of row \(j_t\).
If a tile \(V\in\mathcal R\) that appears before row \(j_t\) meets a cell
of \(R_{j_t}\), its column interval must be contained in
\([\pi(j_t)+2,\,n]\); otherwise it would also contain the hole
\((j_t,\pi(j_t))\).  Hence such a tile cannot cover \(d_t\), and a new
tile of \(\mathcal R\) is forced for each \(t\).  Distinct values of \(t\)
yield distinct tiles, giving  

\[
|\mathcal R|\ge \ell=n-1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.3  Total lower bound

Combining the two independent estimates,

\[
\#\text{tiles}=|\mathcal L|+|\mathcal R|\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Minimality

The construction of Section 1 uses exactly \(2n-2\) tiles, and the
inequality of Section 2 shows that no tiling can use fewer.  Therefore the
minimum possible number of tiles for a \(2025\times2025\) grid is  

\[
2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
